title: Following the moving origin: a testable zeta experiment

voice.style: clear, curious, measured; original narrator without an imitation of any real person
voice.timingRule: Fit each narration clip inside its assigned scene, targeting at least 0.7 seconds of end silence. Rephrase or modestly adjust delivery if a real clip exceeds its scene; word-count estimates are not measured audio durations.

presenter.name: Compass
presenter.construction: Native vector shapes: rounded midnight-blue body, small ivory circular face, two simple charcoal eyes, teal triangular pointer hand, amber circular wrist accent. No recognizable real-person or branded-character likeness.
presenter.behavior: Points to one concept at a time, turns toward the plot during measured results, uses restrained gestures and speech bubbles.
presenter.placement: Small lower-left presenter within x=80..300, y=720..1000; the main scientific visual occupies the center and right. Never obscure axes, labels, or status text.

visualStyle.text: high-contrast large type; short speech bubbles; mathematical labels retained separately from narration
trajectoryLegend: exit marker: last in-view state, labeled with its own target

layout.notes: Keep the presenter small and lower-left. Use at most two short bubble messages per scene, one at a time. Break long formulas across lines. These are design targets; inspect the actual rendered frames before acceptance.

scenes.title: One question inside a work bubble
scenes.narration: First, put one question inside a Warp: an isolated, reversible piece of work. It is a project boundary, not a mathematical force. We test the animation before building its explanation.
bubbles: Test the animation, then explain it
visuals: Three nested-outline cards labeled Coordinator, Scientific animation, and Presentation. Present the animation and presentation as separate linked scopes, not physical universes.
Original geometric presenter points from a question card to a check card. An arrow from accepted animation to presentation establishes the production order.

scenes.title: Move the output origin
scenes.narration: Your idea gave each point its own origin. Here we shift zeta's output origin smoothly from zero toward one. That turns two separate pictures into one changing equation.
visuals: Side-by-side input plane s and output plane w=ζ(s). A labeled target a travels on the output real axis from 0 to 1.
Draw four phase sectors around the moving output origin. Keep the input axes fixed; do not animate a translation of s.

scenes.title: Where the pieces came from
scenes.narration: Wegert's phase plots explain the color view. Lester's work places zeta's a-points in an established research area. We connect those ideas to our earlier two-state switch, using classical prediction and Newton correction.
visuals: Four source cards: earlier switch checkpoint f24b64c; Wegert phase plots (2010), arXiv:1007.2295; Lester a-points (2014), arXiv:1402.0169; classical derivative prediction and Newton correction.
Our four-bin palette is a quantization choice; we do not claim Wegert used it. We use the a-point research subject, not Lester's distribution theorems.

scenes.title: Partial results we can learn from
scenes.narration: Platt and Trudgian provide rigorous finite checks. Lamzouri's preprint presents a proportion bound; OpenAI reports a zero-free region and formalization. These concern zeta zeros, not a certificate for our moving nonzero targets.
visuals: Three readable source cards distinguish Platt–Trudgian interval verification, Lamzouri's September 2026 preprint and its Claude/Anthropic background, and OpenAI's reported zero-free region/Lean formalization.
Label the preprint as a preprint and the Lean work as reported, not replayed here. Do not show a progress bar for RH, adopt these claims as assumptions, or imply they govern ζ(s)=a for nonzero a.

scenes.title: Follow one solution continuously
scenes.narration: We follow the same root as the target moves. Where zeta prime is nonzero, this formula gives its direction and speed. Smaller steps and corrections help the computation stay on track.
bubbles: Track identity; do not jump branches
visuals: Use scientific-animation assets for three labeled starting zeros. Show one short tangent prediction arrow followed by a small correction.
A small target slider advances smoothly. Distinguish the numerical predictor from the accepted corrected sample.

scenes.title: What happened in the chosen window?
scenes.narration: Independent checks find two paths leaving the right edge before the target reaches one. The third reaches a finite one-point. Leaving our window means the view ended, not that the mathematical branch stopped.
formulas: Z1 exits near a = 0.854448; Z2 near a = 0.917225
visuals: Reserved data scene: three branch summary rows with endpoint, exit target, and diagnostic state blank until the independent reference artifact is accepted.
When finalized, show actual reference paths. Any frozen exit marker must say exited at a=... and must not appear to follow the current target.
scenes.finalizationRule: Finalized from passed reference and accepted animation.

scenes.title: Give each method a specific job
scenes.narration: Color shows phase. Continuation follows a solution. Higher precision checks numerical stability. Analytic estimates would be needed for a certificate. These methods help separate tracked connections from artifacts of switching or coarse pixels.
visuals: Four aligned cards feed one evidence ledger: phase view, labeled trajectory, independent high-precision comparison, and an explicitly future analytic certificate.
Show a false line across the old selector jump fading out, beside the actual continuous path. Do not show a certificate check mark unless a certified artifact exists.

scenes.title: A claim the experiment can reject
scenes.narration: Our conjecture required all three paths to remain inside the window. The computed exits give numerical counterevidence. A rigorous rejection would require certified continuation bounds. We keep the original window.
formulas: For all a ∈ [0,1]: s_j(a) ∈ R and ζ′(s_j(a)) ≠ 0
visuals: Show the original conjecture on a card with separate in-window, noncritical, and endpoint clauses.
Reserve the outcome stamp until final reference data arrives. If an exit occurs, highlight the failed in-window clause; do not imply a failure of RH or of ζ itself.
scenes.finalizationRule: Original rectangle preserved; numerical counterevidence is not a certified theorem.

scenes.title: The missing global constraint
scenes.narration: One-points are not zeta zeros. Even three successful paths would not exclude an unseen zero off the critical line. A proof of Riemann needs a global constraint, beyond what these pictures establish.
bubbles: A 1-point is not a zeta zero
formulas: RH target: ζ(ρ) = 0 and 0 < Re ρ < 1 ⇒ Re ρ = 1/2
Three finite paths do not prove this universal statement
visuals: Zoom from the finite window to a symbolic unbounded critical strip. Keep the tested window small and visibly bounded.
Presenter sets a checked experiment card beside an open global-proof card. Do not show a victory check, solved badge, or percentage of RH completed.

sources.title: Elias Wegert, Phase Plots of Complex Functions: a Journey in Illustration
sources.reuse: Phase-coloring foundation. Our four-quadrant palette is a quantization choice, not a claimed reproduction of Wegert's palette.

sources.title: Stephen J. Lester, a-Points of the Riemann zeta-function on the critical line
sources.reuse: Established research on nonzero zeta a-points. We do not implement its distribution theorems.

sources.title: Platt and Trudgian, The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3·10^12
sources.reuse: Rigorous interval verification through height 3·10^12. Our height-10-to-30 animation adds no new verified RH height.

sources.title: Lamzouri, A new proof that more than 2/3 of the zeros are simple and on the critical line
sources.reuse: September 2026 preprint states >67.25% simple and on line. It describes earlier Claude/Anthropic work verified by Alpöge and Furman. We have not independently checked these proofs; this is not a journal-acceptance or percent-RH-solved claim.

sources.title: OpenAI math repository, The quasi-Riemann hypothesis: formalization scope
sources.reuse: OpenAI reports a zero-free half-plane Re(s)>7/8 and Lean formalization. We did not replay that formalization or verify its new proof. It is not an assumption in this experiment.

sources.title: NIST DLMF 25.10(i), Riemann zeta zeros
sources.reuse: RH concerns all nontrivial zeta zeros and the input critical line.

sources.title: mpmath zeta-function documentation
sources.reuse: Zeta values, derivatives, Euler–Maclaurin evaluation and zero seeds; reference environment pins mpmath 1.3.0.

sources.title: Earlier tested two-state zeta laboratory
sources.reuse: Two fixed output origins lead to ζ−a. Its discontinuous selector is not a continuation algorithm.

guardrails: Do not narrate preliminary measurements as accepted results.
A boundary exit is a limitation of the chosen window, not an end of the mathematical branch.
Low sampled derivative or solver failure is not proof of a critical encounter.
One-points off the critical line do not contradict RH.
No novelty, partial RH proof, or likely breakthrough is claimed.
Warp describes the reversible work scope only.

resultSummary.conjectureAssessment: Numerical counterevidence to all three branches remaining in the original rectangle; not interval-certified.
resultSummary.interpretation: Two first-detected right-boundary exits and one finite target-one endpoint; an exit does not end the mathematical branch.
